questiontext.text: The transitive closure of a graph records, for every ordered pair (u, v), whether:

answer.text: v is reachable from u by some directed path

feedback.text: Correct — closure answers reachability for every pair.

answer.text: There is a direct edge from u to v

feedback.text: No — that is the adjacency matrix, not the closure.

answer.text: The shortest-path distance from u to v

feedback.text: No — closure records reachability (yes/no), not distances.

answer.text: u and v share a common neighbor

feedback.text: No — closure is about reachability along paths of any length.

generalfeedback.text: The transitive closure is the reachability matrix: entry (u, v) is 1 exactly when a directed path from u to v exists (of any length).

questiontext.text: Which classic algorithm computes the transitive closure using boolean matrix operations?

answer.text: Warshall's algorithm — the boolean version of Floyd-Warshall

feedback.text: Correct — Warshall's is the boolean OR/AND analogue.
No — Kruskal's builds a minimum spanning tree.
No — Prim's also builds a minimum spanning tree.
No — Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths, not closure.

generalfeedback.text: Warshall's algorithm mirrors Floyd-Warshall but replaces min/+ with logical OR/AND: reach[i][j] |= reach[i][k] && reach[k][j].

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of Warshall's transitive-closure algorithm on V vertices?

feedback.text: Correct — three nested loops over the vertices.
No — that is a single BFS/DFS; Warshall's is cubic.
No — the intermediate-vertex loop adds a third factor of V.
No — Warshall's uses a dense triple loop, not edge sorting.

generalfeedback.text: Warshall's runs three nested loops (intermediate k, source i, target j) over V vertices, giving O(V^3).

questiontext.text: Besides Warshall's algorithm, how else can the full transitive closure be computed?

answer.text: Run BFS or DFS from every vertex and record all vertices reached

feedback.text: Correct — one traversal per source gives that source's reachable set.

answer.text: Run a single DFS from one vertex

feedback.text: No — that only gives reachability from one source, not all pairs.
No — sorting edges does not compute reachability.
No — a topological order alone does not give pairwise reachability.

generalfeedback.text: Launching BFS/DFS from each of the V vertices records that vertex's reachable set; together they form the closure in O(V(V + E)) time.

questiontext.text: The transitive closure is also called the reachability matrix of the graph.

feedback.text: Correct — the closure is exactly the reachability matrix.
The transitive closure and the reachability matrix are the same thing.

questiontext.text: The transitive closure stores the exact shortest-path distance between every pair of vertices.

feedback.text: No — it stores only reachability (a boolean), not distances.
Correct — closure records only whether a path exists, not its length.

questiontext.text: Entry (u, v) of the transitive closure is 1 exactly when v is ______ from u (fill in the English word).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Accepted — Warshall's algorithm computes it.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the transitive closure are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Warshall's algorithm computes it in O(V^3) using boolean OR/AND

feedback.text: Yes — it is the boolean form of Floyd-Warshall.

answer.text: Running BFS/DFS from each vertex also yields the closure

feedback.text: Yes — each source's reachable set forms one row.

answer.text: It records edge weights rather than reachability

feedback.text: No — it records reachability (booleans), not weights.

answer.text: It can be computed in O(V + E) with a single traversal

feedback.text: No — one traversal gives only one source's reachability, not all pairs.

generalfeedback.text: The closure is a reachability matrix computable by Warshall's O(V^3) boolean algorithm or by per-vertex BFS/DFS. It stores booleans, not weights, and needs work per source.
